{{about|balance equations in probability theory|the concept of balanced equations in chemistry|chemical equation}}

In [[probability theory]], a '''balance equation''' is an [[equation]] that describes the probability flux associated with a [[Markov chain]] in and out of states or set of states.<ref name="harr">{{Cite book | last1 = Harrison | first1 = Peter G. | author-link1 = Peter G. Harrison | last2 = Patel | first2 = Naresh M. | title = Performance Modelling of Communication Networks and Computer Architectures | publisher = Addison-Wesley | year = 1992 | isbn = 0-201-54419-9 | url-access = registration | url = https://archive.org/details/performancemodel0000harr }}</ref>

==Global balance==

The '''global balance equations''' (also known as '''full balance equations'''<ref name="kelly">{{cite book |title=Reversibility and stochastic networks |last=Kelly |first=F. P. |author-link=Frank Kelly (mathematician) |year=1979 |publisher=J. Wiley |isbn=0-471-27601-4 |url=http://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~frank/BOOKS/kelly_book.html }}</ref>) are a set of equations that characterize the [[equilibrium distribution]] (or any stationary distribution) of a Markov chain, when such a distribution exists. 

For a [[continuous time Markov chain]] with state space <math>\mathcal{S}</math>, transition rate from state <math>i</math> to <math>j</math> given by <math>q_{ij}</math> and equilibrium distribution given by <math>\pi</math>, the global balance equations are given  by<ref>{{cite conference | first = K.M. | last = Chandy | author-link = K. Mani Chandy | title = The analysis and solutions for general queueing networks  | book-title = Proc. Sixth Annual Princeton Conference on Information Sciences and Systems, Princeton U. | pages = 224&ndash;228 | date = March 1972 | location = Princeton, N.J. }}</ref>

::<math>  \pi_i \sum_{j \in S\setminus \{i\}} q_{ij} = \sum_{j \in S\setminus \{i\}} \pi_j q_{ji}.</math>

for all <math>i \in S</math>. Here <math>\pi_i q_{ij}</math> represents the probability flux from state <math>i</math> to state <math>j</math>. So the left-hand side represents the total flow from out of state ''i'' into states other than ''i'', while the right-hand side represents the total flow out of all states <math>j \neq i</math> into state <math>i</math>. In general it is computationally intractable to solve this system of equations for most queueing models.<ref name="grass">{{cite book |title=Computational probability |last=Grassman |first=Winfried K. |year=2000 |publisher=Springer |isbn=0-7923-8617-5 }}</ref>

==Detailed balance==

{{See also|Detailed balance}}

For a [[continuous time Markov chain]] (CTMC) with [[transition rate matrix]] <math>Q</math>, if <math>\pi_i</math> can be found such that for every pair of states <math>i</math> and <math>j</math>

::<math>\pi_i q_{ij} = \pi_j q_{ji}</math>

holds, then by summing over <math>j</math>, the global balance equations are satisfied and <math>\pi</math> is the stationary distribution of the process.<ref name="boch">{{Cite book | last1 = Bocharov| first1 = Pavel Petrovich| last2 = D'Apice| first2 = C.| last3 = Pechinkin| first3 = A.V.| last4 = Salerno| first4 = S.| title = Queueing theory| publisher = Walter de Gruyter| year = 2004| page = 37| isbn = 90-6764-398-X}}</ref> If such a solution can be found the resulting equations are usually much easier than directly solving the global balance equations.<ref name="grass" />

A CTMC is reversible if and only if the detailed balance conditions are satisfied for every pair of states <math>i</math> and <math>j</math>.

A [[discrete time Markov chain]] (DTMC) with transition matrix <math>P</math> and equilibrium distribution <math>\pi</math> is said to be in detailed balance if for all pairs <math>i</math> and <math>j</math>,<ref>{{cite book |title=Markov Chains |last=Norris |first=James R. |author-link=James R. Norris |year=1998 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |isbn=0-521-63396-6 |url=http://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~james/Markov/ |access-date=2010-09-11}}</ref>

::<math>\pi_i p_{ij} = \pi_j p_{ji}.</math>

When a solution can be found, as in the case of a CTMC, the computation is usually much quicker than directly solving the global balance equations.

==Local balance==

In some situations, terms on either side of the global balance equations cancel. The global balance equations can then be partitioned to give a set of '''local balance equations''' (also known as '''partial balance equations''',<ref name="kelly" /> '''independent balance equations'''<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Baskett | first1 = F. | last2 = Chandy | first2 = K. Mani | author2-link = K. Mani Chandy | last3 = Muntz | first3 = R.R. | last4 = Palacios | first4 = F.G. | title = Open, closed and mixed networks of queues with different classes of customers | journal = Journal of the ACM | volume = 22 | pages = 248&ndash;260 | year = 1975 | issue = 2 | doi = 10.1145/321879.321887| doi-access = free }}</ref> or '''individual balance equations'''<ref name="whittle">{{Cite journal | last1 = Whittle | first1 = P. | author-link = Peter Whittle (mathematician)| title = Equilibrium Distributions for an Open Migration Process | journal = Journal of Applied Probability | volume = 5 | issue = 3 | pages = 567–571 | doi = 10.2307/3211921 | jstor = 3211921| year = 1968 }}</ref>).<ref name="harr" /> These balance equations were first considered by [[Peter Whittle (mathematician)|Peter Whittle]].<ref name="whittle" /><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Chao | first1 = X. | last2 = Miyazawa | first2 = M. | title = On Quasi-Reversibility and Local Balance: An Alternative Derivation of the Product-Form Results | journal = Operations Research | volume = 46 | issue = 6 | pages = 927–933 | doi = 10.1287/opre.46.6.927 | jstor = 222945| year = 1998 }}</ref> The resulting equations are somewhere between detailed balance and global balance equations. Any solution <math>\pi</math> to the local balance equations is always a solution to the global balance equations (we can recover the global balance equations by summing the relevant local balance equations), but the converse is not always true.<ref name="kelly" /> Often, constructing local balance equations is equivalent to removing the outer summations in the global balance equations for certain terms.<ref name="harr" />

During the 1980s it was thought local balance was a requirement for a [[product-form solution|product-form equilibrium distribution]],<ref>{{Cite journal | first1 = Richard J. | last1 = Boucherie | first2 = N.M. | last2 = van Dijk | title = Local balance in queueing networks with positive & negative customers | journal = Annals of Operations Research | year = 1994 | pages = 463&ndash;492 | volume = 48 | issue = 5 | doi=10.1007/bf02033315| url = https://www.researchgate.net/publication/225825899| hdl = 1871/12327 | hdl-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | first1 = K. Mani | last1 = Chandy | author-link1 = K. Mani Chandy | first2 = J.H. Jr | last2 = Howard | first3 = D.F. | last3 = Towsley | title = Product form and local balance in queueing networks | journal = Journal of the ACM | year = 1977 | pages = 250&ndash;263 | volume = 24 | issue = 2 | doi=10.1145/322003.322009| doi-access = free }}</ref> but [[Erol Gelenbe|Gelenbe]]'s [[G-network]] model showed this not to be the case.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.2307/3214781 | title = G-Networks with Triggered Customer Movement | first = Erol | last = Gelenbe | author-link = Erol Gelenbe | journal = Journal of Applied Probability | volume = 30 | issue = 3 | date = Sep 1993 | pages = 742–748 | jstor = 3214781}}</ref>
